analysis.one_liner: Extends Do Not Call protections to all phones and makes robocallers easier to sue.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 15, 2026 by Sen. Durbin with 5 cosponsors and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has had no hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill expands federal Do Not Call rules so they cover every phone subscriber, not just residential landlines, which would bring cell phones under the registry's protection. It makes a single unwanted call enough to sue over — today a caller must break the rules more than once in a year — and turns the $500-per-violation penalty into a floor rather than a ceiling. It also broadens the legal definition of an "automatic telephone dialing system" to include machines that dial from a list of numbers, undoing court decisions that had narrowed which robocall equipment is regulated.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who owns a phone. Cell phone users — who today are largely outside the Do Not Call registry's residential-line coverage — would gain full protection, and anyone getting illegal sales calls would find it much easier to sue and collect $500 per call. The bill directs the FCC to update its regulations within 270 days of enactment [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Do Not Call rules to all telephone subscribers by striking 'residential' throughout the statute, so cell phones and other lines are covered, not just home landlines [S2].
Makes a single illegal call by an entity actionable, replacing the current requirement that the same entity call more than once within any 12-month period, so one violation is enough to sue [S2].
Strikes 'up to' from the damages provision, converting the $500-per-violation penalty from a cap into a floor that courts can exceed, which raises the price of breaking the rules [S2].

Expands the definition of 'automatic telephone dialing system' to cover equipment that dials from a list of telephone numbers, reversing the effect of court rulings that had limited the law to number generators, so more robocall equipment falls under the statute [S2].
Requires the FCC to revise its regulations within 270 days of enactment to implement the expanded rules [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketers, debt collectors, and any business that mass-dials or texts customers. Under the bill, a single call to a number on the expanded registry could trigger a $500 minimum penalty per violation in a private lawsuit, and ordinary list-dialing equipment would count as a regulated autodialer [S2]. Those costs would fall on the calling industry and could be passed along in prices for services that rely on outbound calling.

drawbacks.text: Expanding the autodialer definition to any system that dials 'a list of telephone numbers' could sweep in businesses making ordinary, lawful calls — appointment reminders, fraud alerts, school notifications — exposing them to class-action liability under a law written for telemarketers [S2].

One-call liability with a penalty floor rather than a cap means a single mistake by a caller becomes a lawsuit worth $500 or more per violation, with no warning or cure period; critics of such private rights of action argue the cost lands heavily on legitimate callers and litigation, not on the worst robocallers, who ignore court judgments anyway [S2].

The largest illegal robocall operations are often overseas or judgment-proof, so easier lawsuits mostly deter and tax domestic, reachable businesses rather than the scam callers consumers most want stopped [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — putting cell phones under the Do Not Call registry — is a clear, low-cost gain for consumers that simply closes a coverage gap. The more aggressive provisions are the one-call trigger, the uncapped-above-$500 damages, and the list-dialer autodialer definition: together they shift real litigation risk onto legitimate callers as well as abusers, and they do little against offshore scam operations that are already beyond the reach of U.S. courts. A well-designed version would pair the registry expansion with a safe harbor for informational calls; this bill does not include one in the text provided.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any further action since the day it was introduced.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the Protecting American Consumers from Robocalls Act on April 15, 2026, joined by five original cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; the full action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote since [S4].
The bill has five cosponsors — three Democrats (Smith, Hirono, Welch) and two independents (Sanders, King) — and no Republican sponsor on record [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the mass-calling industry is better off: it continues to operate under the current, narrower rules while the bill sits in committee, and phone users remain without the expanded protections.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred; all six sponsors are Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats, and no Republican has signed on, so the partisan shape is not yet tested.

industries.note: The bill makes every call to a number covered by the expanded registry a sueable violation at $500 or more per call, directly raising the cost of their outbound calling model [S2]. Consumers' interest in fewer sales calls runs directly against this industry's revenue.

Collectors rely heavily on autodialed calls and texts to reach borrowers; classifying list-dialers as autodialers and allowing suits on a single call would sharply increase their legal exposure [S2]. Their interest in maximum call volume conflicts with consumers' interest in fewer unwanted calls.

industries.industry: Businesses that contact customers by phone or text (appointments, alerts, service notices)
industries.note: These callers gain nothing from the bill but would share the added liability if list-dialing equipment counts as an autodialer, even when their calls are welcome; that cost could surface in higher prices or fewer courtesy calls [S2].
A broader private right of action with a damages floor creates more cases to bring on behalf of call recipients; their financial gain depends on the same enforcement consumers would use [S2].

analysis.trajectory: This is where most bills stop. The Senate Commerce Committee is chaired by a Republican, the bill has no Republican cosponsors, and it has shown no movement since its April 2026 referral. Unless it picks up bipartisan support or gets folded into a larger telecom or consumer package before the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027, it will die quietly in committee and would need to be reintroduced from scratch.
